documentation.range: This species is found only on Java and Bali, where its widespread and common (L. Grismer, J. McGuire and E. Quah pers. comm. 2017).
documentation.population: This species is common throughout Java (J. McGuire pers. obs., L. Grismer, E. Quah and J. McGuire pers. comm. 2017).
documentation.habitats: This species inhabits lowland and submontane forests, as well as urbanized areas from sea level to 1,500 m asl. This diurnal, arboreal species is associated with the trunks of large trees. It feeds on ants and possibly other small arthropods. Clutches have 2 to 6 eggs, and the incubation period lasts 26 to 29 days (Das 2010).
documentation.threats: This species is found in the pet trade, but is not thought to be subject to significant threats (L. Grismer and E. Quah pers. comm. 2017)
documentation.measures: Given the high density and wide distribution of this species throughout Java and Bali, no conservation measures are necessary at this point in time (L. Grismer and E. Quah pers. comm. 2017)
documentation.use_trade: The name Draco volans is widely applied to Draco species advertised for sale online in the international pet trade, including those originating outside Java. As such the scale of exploitation of D. volans sensu stricto is unclear, but these animals are not common in trade and are not widely captive-bred.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern on the basis that this species appears to be common and widespread throughout Java and Bali, it adapts well to habitat disturbance so long as suitable trees remain, and no major threats have been identified.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
The name Draco volans has a complex taxonomic history summarized by McGuire and Alcala (2000), with competing taxonomic arrangements presented by Inger (1983), Musters (1983) and Alcala (1986). Ross and Lazell (1991) reported that a number of Philippine taxa synonymized within D. volans by Hennig (1936), Inger (1983) and Musters (1983) occur in sympatry with no evidence of intergradation, and consequently recognized these as full species. This arrangement was followed by McGuire and Alcala (2000), who conducted the first comprehensive modern taxonomic assessment of Philippine Draco and recognized ten species from this archipelago, most of which had variously been considered synonyms or subspecies of D. volans or D. spilopterus.
As most taxonomic attention has focused on the complicated systematics of Philippine taxa (McGuire and Kiew 2001) the true identity of D. volans itself, which has a type locality on Java and which was removed from the Philippine fauna by McGuire and Alcala (2000), remained unclear until a subsequent revision of Southeast Asian Draco lizards by McGuire and Kiew (2001). These authors recognized D. sumatranus, D. boschmai and D. timoriensis - previously treated as either junior synonyms (Inger 1983) or subspecies (Musters 1983) of D. volans - as distinct species on the basis of allopatric distributions and morphological differences, restricting D. volans sensu stricto to Java and Bali. These authors noted that both D. boschmai and D. timoriensis as consequently defined represented species complexes in need of further taxomomic resolution.
